passage: Gautam planted a sunflower seed in the pot beside our stairs on Monday. On Thursday morning I found him kneeling there with his fingers deep in the soil. "Just checking if it's growing," he said. He lifted the seed out, and I saw a thin white thread coming from it, so small. He set it back, pressed the soil down and looked pleased. The next week nothing came up. Gautam dug again and found the seed brown and soft. He looked at it for a long time and said, "I should have waited." I couldn't tell if he was sad or just surprised. - Deepika

qa.q: How many days after planting did Gautam dig up the seed?
qa.a: Gautam dug up the seed on Thursday morning, after planting it on Monday.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling when he found the brown seed?
qa.a: Sad and regretful, though Deepika could not tell whether he was sad or just surprised.

qa.q: What could Gautam do instead of digging while he waits, and why?
qa.a: He could water gently and mark days on a calendar, or grow a second seed in a clear cup to watch, so he can look without disturbing it.

qa.q: How does Deepika see what happened to Gautam's seed?
qa.a: Deepika is sympathetic and cannot tell what Gautam felt, but notes how long he looked at the seed.

grounding: A boy digs up a seed after three days to check on it, kills the tiny root and learns that some things need patient waiting.

passage:
Monday: Gurpreet planted a sunflower seed in a yogurt cup and set it on the windowsill. His friend Tarun said sunflowers grow as tall as doors.
Thursday: Nothing showed. Gurpreet couldn't stand it. He tipped the soil into his palm and found the seed. A tiny white root, thinner than a thread, was poking out. "It's working!" He pushed it back in, a little crooked, and pressed the soil down hard.
The next Thursday: Still nothing. He dug again, gently this time. The white root was brown and shrivelled. Tarun's sunflower, which Tarun had never touched, had two green leaves. Gurpreet planted a new seed and wrote WAIT on the cup in marker.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet find when he tipped out the soil on Thursday?
qa.a: A tiny white root, thinner than a thread, poking out of the seed.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel on Thursday before digging?
qa.a: He was impatient and couldn't stand waiting any longer.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do to see roots without harming the plant?
qa.a: Grow a spare seed on wet cotton or in a clear cup, so he can watch the root without digging.

qa.q: What would change if Gurpreet had left the seed alone, like Tarun?
qa.a: It would likely have grown leaves too, as Tarun's untouched sunflower did.

grounding: Over two weeks, a boy digs up his seed too soon, kills the new root and learns to wait.

passage: Charu, you've checked your seeds four times today. Sit down. When I, Mohit, was eight, my father gave me three pea seeds and a corner of our field. I planted them in the morning. That evening I was back, staring at the mud. On the third day I couldn't bear it. I dug up the middle one with my fingers. There it was, a little white tail curling out. I was so pleased I ran to show my father. He looked and said nothing. I pushed it back in. That one never came up. The other two, the ones I left alone, climbed the fence by the end of the month. Only then did my father say, "Some things you can't hurry."

qa.q: How many pea seeds did the father give?
How did young Mohit feel on the third day?
qa.a: So impatient he couldn't bear it, and then pleased to see the root.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story cost Mohit a plant?
qa.a: Digging up the middle seed; leaving it alone like the other two would have let it grow.

qa.q: How might Mohit's father have felt when shown the root?
qa.a: He said nothing, perhaps already expecting it would not survive and letting the lesson come on its own.

grounding: An elder recalls digging up a seed after three days, killing its root, and learning that growth needs patience.
